cards.explanation: The answer is the nations. The writer says, “make known His deeds among the nations.” God's wonders weren't meant to stay in a back room, friends. I'd have trouble keeping good news quiet myself, and I once told a whole line of strangers about a perfect batch.

The answer is False. The verse says, “tell of all His wonders.” Not a few of them, not the top three. When you've got a long list of wonders, friends, you've got a long song to sing, and that sounds like a good problem to me.

The answer is always. The verse says, “Seek out the LORD and His strength; seek His face always.” Always means every day, not just the days that feel special. That's a lot like my ovens, which stay warm whether or not anybody's coming.

The answer is the wonders He has done. Verse 5 says, “Remember the wonders He has done, His marvels, and the judgments He has pronounced…” The writer points straight at what God has done, friends. Memory gets put to work on the good stuff.
The answer is False. Verse 7 says, “His judgments carry throughout the earth.” Not a corner of the map, the whole earth. And notice the writer says “…the LORD our God…” so he counts himself in.

The answer is His covenant. Verse 8 says, “He remembers His covenant forever, the word He ordained for a thousand generations…” A covenant is a solemn promise God made. And He's the one remembering, friends, which is more than I can say for my oven timer.

The answer is the land of Canaan. Verse 11 gives God's words: “I will give you the land of Canaan as the portion of your inheritance.” A portion is a share, and an inheritance is a gift handed down. This one came with a promise attached.

The answer is that they wander from nation to nation. Verse 13 says, “…they wandered from nation to nation, from one kingdom to another.” Verse 12 calls them few in number, few indeed, and strangers in the land. A small family on the move, friends.

The answer is True. Verse 14 says it plainly: “He let no man oppress them…” A small family wandering through other people's kingdoms, and God kept watch over them. Few in number didn't mean unprotected, friends.

The answer is kings. Verse 14 says, “He rebuked kings on their behalf…” God Himself stepped in for His people. Verse 15 gives His words: “Do not touch My anointed ones! Do no harm to My prophets!” A small family had the biggest backup there is.

The answer is False. Verse 17 says God sent a man before them, “Joseph, sold as a slave.” Verse 18 adds, “They bruised his feet with shackles and placed his neck in irons…” so this was a hard road. I think this part of the story hurts, friends.

The answer is the word of the LORD. Verse 19 says Joseph stayed in irons “…until his prediction came true and the word of the LORD proved him right.” The one doing the proving is the word of the LORD, friends. His prediction came true, and that's when the irons stopped.

The answer is the king. Verse 20 says, “The king sent and released him; the ruler of peoples set him free.” Verse 18 had Joseph in irons, so this is a big change from shackles, friends. The king is the one who sent and released him.

The answer is wisdom. Verse 22 gives the purpose of Joseph's appointment: “…to instruct his princes as he pleased and teach his elders wisdom.” Verse 20 had him set free, and verse 21 makes him master of the king's household. That's quite a turn for a man who had been in irons, friends.

The answer is Egypt. Verse 23 says, “Then Israel entered Egypt; Jacob dwelt in the land of Ham.” The psalm uses both names, Israel and Jacob, in that one verse. Egypt is the next stop in the story, friends.

The answer is that He makes them very fruitful. Verse 24 says, “…the LORD made His people very fruitful, more numerous than their foes…” The family that was once few in number is growing. God's blessing in Egypt shows up in the numbers, friends.

The answer is True. Verse 24 says God made His people “…more numerous than their foes…” Remember when they were few indeed? That's a real turnaround, friends. The headcount changed, and God's the one who changed it.

The answer is that God turned them to hate His people. Verse 25 says of Israel's foes, “…whose hearts He turned to hate His people, to conspire against His servants.” It's a hard line, and the text states it plainly. I think this is where the story gets heavy, friends.

The answer is that they perform His miraculous signs. Verse 26 says God sent Moses His servant, and Aaron, whom He had chosen. Then verse 27 says, “They performed His miraculous signs among them, and wonders in the land of Ham.” Moses and Aaron were sent to do what God gave them to do, friends.
The answer is that the fish die off. Verse 29 says, “He turned their waters to blood and caused their fish to die.” It's a heavy plague for the land, friends. The fish did not make it.

The answer is True. Verse 33 says, “He struck their vines and fig trees and shattered the trees of their country.” Vines, fig trees and the trees of their country all took the hit. It comes right after the hail and lightning of verse 32.

The answer is every plant in their land. Verse 35 says, “They devoured every plant in their land and consumed the produce of their soil.” Every plant, and the produce too, friends. That's a total sweep.

The answer is False. Verse 37 says, “He brought Israel out with silver and gold, and none among His tribes stumbled.” So Israel left with silver and gold. Empty-handed doesn't fit that verse, friends, and neither does a single stumble.
The answer is glad. Verse 38 says, “Egypt was glad when they departed, for the dread of Israel had fallen on them.” The text gives that reason itself, friends. Egypt was glad to see them go.

The answer is a cloud and a fire. Verse 39 says, “He spread a cloud as a covering and a fire to light up the night.” A covering and a light for the night, both from God's hand. It was a pretty good setup for a desert walk, friends.

The answer is rock. Verse 41 says, “He opened a rock, and water gushed out; it flowed like a river in the desert.” Water gushing out of a rock in the middle of a desert, friends. The verse says it flowed like a river.

The answer is that He remembered His promise to Abraham. Verse 42 says, “For He remembered His holy promise to Abraham His servant.” The writer gives the reason right there, friends. And verse 8 says He remembers His covenant forever.

The answer is so they would keep His laws. Verse 45 says, “…that they might keep His statutes and obey His laws.” After all those wonders, friends, this is where the song lands. And the very next word is Hallelujah!
